headline: Approved no-parking signs for Karatzas Heights, Maple Street parking changes, and Amoskeag Bridge detour; amended kratom ban recommended for further review.
summary: The committee approved Traffic Division items on stop signs, parking limits, a crosswalk, and a rescinded parking rule. It also approved a detour route for the Amoskeag Bridge westbound rehabilitation project scheduled for 2028/2029. On the kratom ban, the committee amended the ordinance and recommended referral, but a motion to send it to the full Board that night failed.
decisions: Approved the Traffic Division agenda items, including a stop sign at Ash Street at Webster Street, a no commercial vehicles rule on Allen Street, no parking anytime on parts of Jewett Street, a crosswalk on Park Side Avenue, and rescinding no parking on Orange Street.
Approved Jemco Properties LLC's request to install no parking signs in the new Karatzas Heights subdivision extending off Karatzas Avenue.
Approved the detour route for the Amoskeag Bridge westbound rehabilitation project scheduled for 2028/2029.
Approved limiting Maple Street, from Hanover Street to Bridge Street, to a single lane northbound and enacting the related no parking anytime ordinances and rescinding ORD 3355.

Voted to amend the kratom ordinance by removing the “use” and “possession” language, and to recommend that the amended ordinance pass and be referred to the Committee on Bills on Second Reading for technical review. No vote count was given.
Motion to expedite the committee’s report on the kratom ordinance to the full Board failed, 3-1.

## COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SAFETY, HEALTH & TRAFFIC

October 6, 2026 at 5:30 PM

Chairman Vincent called the meeting to order.

The Clerk called the roll.

Present: Aldermen Vincent, Goonan, Dexter, Barry

Absent: Alderman Bonilla

Messrs.: Alderman Trisciani, A. Thomas, M. Davis, E. Rice

1. The Traffic Division has submitted an agenda which needs to be addressed:

STOP SIGN

On Ash Street at Webster Street, NE corner

Alderman Goonan

NO COMMERCIAL VEHICLES

On Allen Street, between Boynton Street and S Main Street

Alderman Barry

NO PARKING ANYTIME

- On Jewett Street, west side, from Cilley Road to a point 140 feet north
- On S Jewett Street, west side, from Cilley Road to a point 120 feet south
- On S Jewett Street, east side, from Cilley Road to a point 120 feet south

Alderman Terrio

CROSSWALK

On Park Side Avenue, south of Putnam Street

Alderman Vincent

RESCIND NO PARKING NOVEMBER 15 - APRIL 15

On Orange Street, south side, from Chestnut Street to Pine Street (ORD 9457)

Alderman Dexter

On motion of Alderman Goonan , duly seconded by Alderman Dexter , it was voted to approve.

2. Communication from Jemco Properties LLC, requesting approval to install no parking signs in the new Karatzas Heights subdivision extending off of Karatzas Avenue.

Chairman Vincent: I spoke with Kristen Clarke in the Traffic Division; she is fine with this.

On motion of Alderman Dexter , duly seconded by Alderman Goonan , it was voted to approve.

On motion of Alderman Dexter , duly seconded by Alderman Goonan , it was voted to expedite the committee’ s report to the full Board.

3. Communication from Caleb Dobbins, Highway Chief Engineer, requesting approval of the following detour route for the Amoskeag Bridge westbound rehabilitation project scheduled for 2028/2029:

• Maintain eastbound traffic on eastbound bridge (single lane), detour westbound traffic over Bridge Street Bridge

• Allow pedestrian/bicycle traffic to utilize the second lane (northern) on eastbound bridge

On motion of Alderman Goonan , duly seconded by Alderman Dexter , it was voted to approve.

4. Communication from the Highway Chief Engineer requesting that Maple Street, from Hanover Street to Bridge Street, be limited to a single lane northbound, and that the following Traffic Ordinances be enacted:

RESCIND NO PARKING ANYTIME

On Maple Street, west side, from Cilley Road to Webster Street (ORD 3355)

NO PARKING ANYTIME

- On Maple Street, west side, from Cilley Road to Hanover Street
- On Maple Street, west side, from a point 60 feet north of Concord Street to

Webster Street

On motion of Alderman Goonan , duly seconded by Alderman Barry , it was voted to approve.

On motion of Alderman Dexter , duly seconded by Alderman Goonan , it was voted to expedite the committee’ s report to the full Board.

- 5. Communication from Aldermen Thomas and Barry requesting approval of an
- Ordinance Amendment banning the substance known as kratom.

Chairman Vincent: There's a lot going on with this, folks. Kratom is a natural therapeutic as it stands on its own but when it's interacted with many other drugs and whatnot, it certainly does become dangerous. There's no question that this needs to be off our streets. I just want to make sure that we are following the proper vetted process to get this done. And when I say proper vetted, I mean we need to include the Clerk's Office, Police Department, Health Department, Solicitor's Office. We want to make sure that we avoid just doing a blanket ordinance, for lack of better words. I want to make sure this is properly done. I don't have a problem pushing this up to Bills on Second Reading, but I do think that we need to make sure that it goes through the process and during that time it does get vetted properly.

Alderman Barry: Actually, what we were going to do and what we were hoping to do is, unfortunately, Alderman Thomas couldn't make it, initially, we were going to put this in the Alcohol, Other Drugs and Youth Services Committee. But because of the fact that she couldn't be here in a timely fashion, our Clerk thought it would be appropriate to put it in Public Safety. Our goal is to get it in front of the full Board tonight, not to go to Bills on Second Reading and so on. I've spoken with Emily Rice. She put a lot of thought and effort into it. She feels confident that the ordinance that we're presenting is strong enough to move forward. I'm going to vote to move forward on it because I think it's that important. At the very least we get it off the shelves in the city of Manchester. The city of Nashua has an ordinance that's age restricted, no one under the age of 21 can possess. And they can't sell it to anyone under 21. Franklin has it just like our ordinance. They can't sell it or possess it anywhere in the town of Franklin. Throughout the country, there are a lot of states that are doing it. Our state on the Senate level and also on the legislative level have bills that are sitting there. And my understanding was they were going to incorporate both the Senate and the legislative bills and coordinate to get that going. They haven't done it yet, but I think for Manchester, it's that important that I think we should lead and we should get them out of our stores, the convenience stores or whatever stores possess them. Even if we give them a 30 day reprieve that they can send it back to the distributor. But, you know, people are dying throughout the country. It's not just from the kratom itself, but it's from added substances that go with it. That's how dangerous this drug is. We've heard from Randy Stevens over at Hope for New Hampshire Recovery, where some of the people that go there have confided in them. One of them, for example, is spending $300 a day on it. That's how addictive this stuff is. And that's how much he relies on it. I think all of us have received emails from people. But when you follow up with the emails, which I did, they're all from out of state. I communicated with a lady from Tennessee who was concerned about our ordinance, but she's from Tennessee. We've got to worry about the city of Manchester. I don't think we should be delaying it. I would certainly make a motion to accept the ordinance and to move it, at the very least, to the full Board tonight so we can discuss it.

Alderman Trisciani: I have concerns with this because this is an incredibly complex issue. And yes, we did get stuff from out of state. We also received an email in state from a doctor. I feel like what we might be doing is creating a culture of unintended consequences with this. I would be fine saying no one under the age of 18 or under the age of 21, but I do have a real concern, similar to the spice epidemic we had many years ago, that as we start calling things out, if we're limiting it to just the synthetics, they're just going to change the makeup to sell it at the store. So you might say we're going to ban this one because it's made of these synthetic products or has these byproducts; they're going to change the recipe. Or if you say, we're going to ban something called Delta-8 or Blue Lotus, they're just going to change the name and rebrand it. My bigger concern is that people should have access to the pure form, the herbal form of it, because that has been shown and has been proven to help people in certain circumstances, whether it's pain management, in some cases it is helping people get off of an addiction. I know Goffstown tried to do this and they deferred to the state level as well. I think there's two bills coming before the state level. And I think our purview, especially, is when it comes to the cost and what is involved in overseeing this. I think to your point, it's not really ready for prime time today to go up to the Board without a further study of the parties that are going to be involved in the city. I would strongly feel that if we're going to go with something like this, it has to be similar to Nashua with an age limit.

Alderman Goonan: I don't think anybody wants kratom as it sits in the streets right now being sold in our stores. I think we're going to get a lot of direction from the state pretty soon, but in the interim, after speaking to Health Director, the Police Department and our Clerk's Office, I think as long as we have that 120 days to try to figure it out after and try to figure out the enforcement part, that's what I was concerned with. How are we going to enforce this? If we can pass this, get it out, and take that 120 days to have our department heads try to figure this out, they're quite capable.

Alderman Barry: Some people have a concern that they're just going to change the recipe on it. Well, good for them. And we can change the ordinance to include it. So we can go back and forth as needed. But that's the way it goes. But in the meantime, at least we get it off our shelves. And the kids, are some people going to be able to get it? If someone is relying on it for medical reasons they can go over to Hooksett and get it. They can go wherever they want to get it, but just not in Manchester. I think we need to focus on our city. I spoke with the Health Director, this stuff isn't regulated. I'm hearing from the experts, I'm hearing from the people, especially the people that work hand in hand with Randy Stevens over at Hope for New Hampshire Recovery. And when he comes forward and he tells us that, and I did forward it to this committee, people that he deals with on a daily basis are coming in and complaining about what it's doing to them. And they're having a tough time getting rid of it. It's just as addictive, they said, as heroin. I just think we're moving in the right direction. Nothing against the state, but why haven't they done anything with it? They've had plenty of time to do it. I just don't think it's appropriate to wait. I think we should act. I'll make a motion to send it to the full Board tonight, but I'm certainly in favor of the ordinance as written.

Alderman Trisciani: One thing that does worry me is saying that they can just go to Hooksett and buy it, but they can't be in possession of it in Manchester. So if someone has to find the pure form for a medical reason, or because it helps them with a better quality of life, now they're not allowed to have that on their possession in Manchester. So they get stopped for speeding, it's in their possession, what happens to them? I just think that the unintended consequences trying to cram this through right now without a proper study or without a proper review process is probably more dangerous to some people who need the pure form of it. I don't believe there's any question that the pure form is fine for people to use. It's just when we get the synthetics. I do think if we're going to cram something like this through, you at least have to have an age restriction or find some better way to do it. I just think we're not ready for prime time at this point.

Alderman Goonan: Is there a reason this is dispensed through a doctor or anything like that for a medical reason as it sits now?

Anna Thomas, Health Director: There's natural kratom and synthetic kratom. So there are people who access natural kratom and can do so responsibly. It is not regulated. This is what happens with other cities and towns across the country, they just have to ban all of it. Because if we do pick up somebody, somebody from law enforcement picks up somebody in arrest, there's no way to test for it. So they won't even be able to validate whether or not someone is actually carrying kratom on them. I think this is really something that is now a national discussion. As you know, you've seen the news on these Ole Miss cases. Those have not been linked to kratom. And I've reached out to Mississippi today actually and tried to speak to people there. They want to make it clear that people are drawing conclusions about these cases. There's a lot of misinformation that's getting thrown around, but it doesn't deter them from messaging about any uncontrolled substance that's out there. They are trying to deter that no matter what and deter people from using it. I think at the end of the day, similar to Alderman Trisciani, I look at it as an age limit, kind of the compromise at this point. That's something you all need to decide. Or you do it incrementally, start with an age limit, and then you could build upon it. The state's talking about passing legislation. The feds, the DEA, is on the cusp of doing their due diligence as well. So, it's up to you guys how much you want to go with this. I just want to be careful that we're doing this as well thought out as we can. And we're all trying to be informed because it's a lot on the City Clerk's office, it's going to be a lot on the police department to manage this and confiscate it off the shelves. Sometimes this stuff is packaged and you don't even know it's kratom. That's the problem. Several of you who are in law enforcement, you know the real deal. When you're on the streets, you know what you're seeing. At the end of the day, it's going to be how fast you want to go with it as a Board. It's your call to do that.

Alderman Barry: Do you agree that the ordinance as written is strong enough?

A. Thomas: I'm not the legal expert. That's what your city solicitor is for, because you need to make it stick in court. You need to also be able to have that as a tool for law enforcement. That's where Chief Marr has to speak to those pieces. I just think if you're going to go ahead and do this, they've done it in other parts of the country. Like I said, the compromise is if you want to start it incrementally and do an age restriction, that's cleaner because clearly nobody wants young people having access to this. That's a big concern for me. I don't even know how much of it is out there in the city of Manchester, and I don't think anybody has a full inventory. I know several businesses carry it, but I don't know what the full inventory is. So all of that's going to have to be accounted for. But right now, a young person of any age can walk into a store and buy this stuff. And that to me is the biggest red flag of all.

Alderman Barry: I want it off the shelves in Manchester. What I don't want is people from Hooksett coming to Manchester to get it. If people in Manchester have to go elsewhere, so be it. That's the way it goes. That could be anything. They want to go to get marijuana in Maine. They can go get it. I don't want people to come into Manchester. I want Manchester to lead in this fight to get it out of our stores so that anyone of any age can't get it. I don't want any age restriction. I want just to get rid of it. I think it should be off our shelves. Nashua has the 21 age restriction; if I was going to compromise, that's the only age that I would compromise to. I wouldn't do 18 because now you're talking about kids that are possibly still in high school and they'll be able to get it. Are they going to be able to get it? Probably, but I don't want them to come to Manchester to get it.

A. Thomas: I contacted AMR, the fire department, police department, all of our first responders, we looked at our overdose data. We're not seeing overdoses and deaths correlated with kratom. However, when you talk to the Doorways, when you talk to Hope for New Hampshire Recovery, I was at the Overdose Fatality Review Commission at the state yesterday, and I talked to the medical examiner, and there were other Doorways there. They're seeing an uptick in patients reporting the use of kratom and some abusing the use of kratom. We're getting these anecdotal feedback from systems. We're not seeing it in overdose and fatalities yet. I did ask the school district. They did not see a huge uptick either. But at the same time, and I think I've said this to several of you now, we are not often in a position to get ahead of something like this. I spend every day chasing down overdoses and fatalities. My staff does. We are not often in a position where we get ahead of something and getting it off the streets.

Alderman Barry: Randy Stevens could not make it, but someone from Hope for New Hampshire Recovery is here to speak.

Michelle Davis, Hope for NH Recovery: In my role, I provide peer support lead groups. And I also oversee our pivot program, which is our crisis housing respite, if you will, that we have at the center. Recently we have seen an influx in kratom relapse, kratom related reoccurrences, which causes not only increases in and the support that we are providing our addicts and those afflicted with addiction, but it's also causing setbacks in their lives completely. It's readily available. They can't go pick up an energy drink without it being at the counter and it's creating stress. And not only that, their children can be susceptible to it now because it's just so readily available.

Alderman Barry: So, what are your thoughts? Did you have a chance to read the ordinance?

M. Davis: I personally did not. Randy contact me very shortly before this meeting. And I was told to come here and represent Hope. Although I can't fill his shoes accurately, I think he did send a memo with his thoughts. Honestly, living and being a new resident of Manchester, I moved here about a year ago. I spent most of my life in California. As somebody in recovery, it should be banned in my opinion. It's not something that many people in our community would turn to. And the therapeutic value of it just doesn't seem to outweigh the risks that it entails.

Alderman Barry: So you're in favor of us banning it?

M. Davis: Absolutely.

Alderman Barry: For everyone, not just people that are under 21. At the very least, get it off the shelves in Manchester. And as far as the possession goes and the enforcement goes, our Clerk's Office can enforce whether someone's selling it or not after the ordinance is ordained. They would have to go to these stores and enforce it and pull their license if they continue to sell it. But as far as the possession goes, we can deal with that. I'm comfortable that once we get this under wraps, we could deal with that. But my goal and my hope is to get it out of our stores in Manchester and make it illegal to sell. So you're in agreement with that?

M. Davis: Absolutely.

Chairman Vincent: Do I have a motion that the ordinance as it's written be referred to Bills on Second Reading for technical review?

Alderman Barry: No. To the full Board tonight.

Chairman Vincent: We have to pass this first and then move it up.

Matthew Normand, City Clerk: Right. The committee’ s recommendation would be to refer the item to the Committee on Bills on Second Reading. That's the next step. If it's unanimous that the committee wants the ordinance be reported to the full Board tonight, it could.

Chairman Vincent: We need approval on the ordinance first.

M. Normand: Every ordinance goes from whatever the originating committee is to the Board and then to Bills on Second Reading is the second step. The motion is the same for every ordinance coming out of an originating committee. If this committee decides unanimously to expedite its report to the full Board, it would be reported tonight.

Alderman Dexter: I have a concern with the words “use ” and “possession ” in the city, those two words in the ordinance as it stands right now. My concern is that somebody can go to Hooksett or Bedford and purchase it, and then it's going to cause more work, more stuff here in Manchester. I'm not opposed to that in the future, but if the goal of this is to get it out of our stores, I think we need to remove those words.

Emily Rice, Solicitor: Yes, that can be taken out if that's what you want to do.

Alderman Dexter: We could always add it later or look at this as we study it with the state. We'll see what the state does with this. But that would be my concern.

Alderman Goonan: I talked to the Police Chief. His question also was, what do they want the police department to do with this? So, I don't disagree.

On motion of Alderman Dexter , duly seconded by Alderman Goonan , it was voted to amend the Ordinance Amendment by removing language related to “use ” and “possession ”, and further that the Ordinance as amended ought to pass and be referred to the Committee on Bills on Second Reading for technical review.

Chairman Vincent: You wanted to make a second motion?

Alderman Barry: To send it to the full Board tonight, and just to reiterate what you said, I also spoke with the Chief. The Chief is absolutely in favor of banning it in the city of Manchester, just so everyone knows.

Chairman Vincent: Nobody's not in favor of banning this. It's just a matter of doing it the correct way, ensuring that all avenues to pursue are explored, and I would encourage that between now and whenever this is done, that the Clerk's Office, Police Department, Health Department, and Solicitor's Office communicate in-depth over this to make sure we get it right. This is not something we want to play games with. We want it off our streets, but we do want to do it the right way as well.

Alderman Barry moved to expedite the committee’ s report to the full Board. Alderman

Dexter duly seconded the motion. Aldermen Barry, Dexter, and Goonan voted yea.

Alderman Vincent voted nay. The motion failed.

M. Normand: The committee’ s report will be on the Board’ s consent agenda on October 20, with a recommendation that it be referred to the Committee on Bills on Second Reading.

There being no further business, on motion of Alderman Dexter , duly seconded by

Alderman Goonan , it was voted to adjourn.

A True Record. Attest.

Clerk of Committee
